interactions.summary: A student asks why someone who did not initiate the betrayal would be punished in the same way as the traitor.
Jiang and students identify the real scandal in the Ugolino episode: the sons are imprisoned and tortured despite doing nothing themselves.
Jiang answers that medieval feud logic killed sons to prevent vengeance, but Dante still marks that necessity as unjust and appeals to a higher law beyond clan retaliation.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante accepts that Ugolino himself betrayed Pisa but is morally shaken by the punishment of Ugolino's innocent sons.
Jiang explains that many cultures of the period killed sons alongside fathers because otherwise the sons became morally obligated to avenge the family line.
Jiang says Dante understands the practical logic of feud prevention but still judges the punishment of sons for a father's crime as unjust.

signature_moments.moment: Dante can see why the feud machine kills sons and still call it unjust.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i understand all this but it's still unjust
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's distinction between historical necessity and higher justice.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The intergenerational vengeance structure Jiang says made killing sons appear politically necessary.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang explicitly situates Dante inside a feud-driven historical world while stressing Dante's appeal to a justice higher than that world.
